blog_summary: Adrian Colyer provides an in-depth overview of Hyperledger Fabric, a permissioned blockchain system with a modular design and a novel execute-order-validate processing pipeline. The paper highlights Fabric's key features, including pluggable components (e.g., consensus algorithms), support for smart contracts in any language, and impressive performance metrics (3500+ tps, sub-second latency). The blog emphasizes Fabric's departure from the traditional order-execute architecture, which suffers from sequential execution bottlenecks and non-determinism issues. Instead, Fabric's three-phase pipeline separates execution, ordering, and validation, enabling parallel execution, better performance, and tolerance for non-deterministic smart contracts. The author praises the paper's clarity and practical insights, noting Fabric's real-world use cases in enterprise asset management, foreign exchange netting, and cross-currency payments.
paper_title: Hyperledger Fabric: A Distributed Operating System for Permissioned Blockchains
paper_abstract: Fabric is a modular and extensible open-source system for deploying and operating permissioned blockchains and one of the Hyperledger projects hosted by the Linux Foundation (www.hyperledger.org). Fabric is the first truly extensible blockchain system for running distributed applications. It supports modular consensus protocols, which allows the system to be tailored to particular use cases and trust models. Fabric is also the first blockchain system that runs distributed applications written in standard, general-purpose programming languages, without systemic dependency on a native cryptocurrency. This stands in sharp contrast to existing blockchain platforms that require “smart-contracts” to be written in domain-specific languages or rely on a cryptocurrency. Fabric realizes the permissioned model using a portable notion of membership, which may be integrated with industry-standard identity management. To support such flexibility, Fabric introduces an entirely novel blockchain design and revamps the way blockchains cope with nondeterminism, resource exhaustion, and performance attacks. This paper describes Fabric, its architecture, the rationale behind various design decisions, its most prominent implementation aspects, as well as its distributed application programming model. We further evaluate Fabric by implementing and benchmarking a Bitcoin-inspired digital currency. We show that Fabric achieves end-to-end throughput of more than 3500 transactions per second in certain popular deployment configurations, with sub-second latency, scaling well to over 100 peers. ∗ Work done at IBM.
